chunk_findings.detail: `bug_globs_of` dereferences `state.bugs[b]` for every id returned by `fixes_of(state, item_id, cfg)` without the existence check its immediate sibling performs. The function defined right below it, `open_bugs_of`, consumes the *same* `fixes_of` result and filters it with `{b for b in named if b in state.bugs}` — i.e. `fixes_of` is known to be able to name ids that are not present in `state.bugs`. Given a fix task whose `fixes` list contains such an id (e.g. a bug id that has no `bug.found` record folded into that worktree's `state.bugs`), `sorted(fixes_of(...))` yields that id and `state.bugs[b]` raises `KeyError`, crashing the `claim` path instead of falling through to `... or None`. The new code in `claim.py` unconditionally calls this helper whenever a task has no globs of its own, so a claim that should just carry the bug's globs (or none) aborts instead.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/completion.py:95 (`bug_globs_of`)

chunk_findings.detail: The new fallback hint tells the user to run `ddflow --agent {ctx.log.agent_id} update {a['id']} --globs …`, i.e. with `--agent` placed *before* the subcommand. In this project the agent flag is only ever accepted *after* the subcommand — every invocation in the change/report uses that form (`ddflow claim --agent X …` in the report, `ddflow update --globs` as the stated workaround, and the test helper is called as `run_cli(repo, "claim", "T1", agent="w")`). With that parser shape (option registered on the subparser), copying the printed command and running it from any tree fails at argument parsing, e.g. `ddflow --agent w update T1 --globs src/h.py` → `error: unrecognized arguments: --agent w`, so the user is handed a remediation command that cannot be executed. Given the intent ("the exact command to run", a command that unblocks the commit hook), the hint should use the same placement as all other invocations (`ddflow update T1 --globs … --agent w`). The new test only string-matches `"ddflow --agent w update T1 --globs"`, so it locks in the malformed form rather than catching it.

chunk_findings.detail: `bug_globs_of` indexes `state.bugs[b]` directly for every id returned by `fixes_of(state, item_id, cfg)`, with no membership check. The sibling helper immediately below is written defensively for exactly that reason: `open_bugs_of` returns `{b for b in named if b in state.bugs}` because `fixes_of` is not guaranteed to yield only ids that exist as bug records (the same `named = fixes_of(...)` result is filtered there). Given a fix task whose `fixes`/bug-link names a bug id that is absent from `state.bugs` (e.g. a link to a removed/unknown bug id), claiming that task with no explicit `--globs` takes the new fallback branch in `claim.py` (`want is None and parked is not None and not parked.globs`), calls `bug_globs_of`, and `state.bugs[b]` raises `KeyError`; the claim crashes with a traceback instead of succeeding or refusing cleanly. Applying the same `if b in state.bugs` guard used by `open_bugs_of` avoids this.

chunk_findings.detail: The reworded block now reads `leased to {ctx.log.agent_id}, ...`, i.e. it asserts that the explicit `--agent` identity actually holds the lease. But the branch condition is unchanged (`owner and d["worktree"] and not d["rebound"]`) and nothing in this diff changes the holder or the identity the commit hook matches on for that branch — the very branch whose reported behaviour (per the intent) is that the claim is "leased under the tree's identity" while printing "not adopted". Concretely: from a tree owned by `parent`, `ddflow claim T1 --agent sub-1` now prints `leased to sub-1 ... not adopted`, while `state(repo).items["T1"].lease.agent` is still `parent` (and the hook still matches the tree identity), so message and behaviour disagree in the opposite direction instead of agreeing. The updated test in tests/test_asagent_tree.py only pins the string (`assert "leased to sub-1" in out`) and `assert not t1.adopted`; it never asserts `t1.lease.agent == "sub-1"` (or the hook identity), so it passes while the message stays unverified. The accompanying advice line (`ddflow --agent {ctx.log.agent_id} update {a['id']} --globs`) compounds this: it tells the user to run an update as `sub-1` from inside the tree the same message just said is `parent`'s, so following it re-enters the identity the claim was filed under and the hook (which checks the tree identity) can still refuse.

chunk_findings.detail: The "held" predicate is `it.lease.holder == me or _in_leased_tree(repo, it.lease.worktree, here)`, so any lease whose tree the caller merely stands in is selected as if the caller held it, and the refusal text hard-asserts the opposite ("{me} holds {len(held)} items"). Concrete input: agent `other` holds a lease on item `build` in tree `T`, agent `me` holds nothing and runs `ddflow heartbeat` (or `ddflow heartbeat ""`, which is exactly the shape of the original bug report) from `T`. `_the_held_item` computes `held == ["build"]`, `len(held) == 1`, and returns `("build", None)`, so the no-id branch proceeds to renew a lease the caller does not hold — silently extending `other`'s lease (defeating `services.leasebreak`'s idle/yield detection and keeping waiters blocked) instead of returning the promised `"heartbeat needs an item id ..., and me holds no lease"`. If the renewal body is instead holder-gated, the caller gets a refusal that names an item it does not hold; either way the message promised by the intent ("list the items the caller holds") is not what the predicate computes. The same OR misfires in the other direction: when `me` really does hold exactly one lease in a tree that also contains another agent's lease, `held` has two entries, so instead of the intended single-item auto-heartbeat the command fails with `"{me} holds 2 items -- ..."`, listing an item that is not the caller's. The tree match should be a fallback for a lease whose recorded holder no longer matches the caller (or be applied only when there is no holder match), not OR-ed unconditionally.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/heartbeat.py:95 (`_the_held_item`)

chunk_findings.detail: The whole point of the new message is that it lists "the items the caller holds" — i.e. leases filtered by the calling agent. None of the three tests can tell that filtering apart from listing *every* lease in the repo: in `test_the_only_held_item_is_renewed_without_naming_it` the only lease in the repo belongs to `w` (T2 is seeded but never claimed), in `test_several_held_items_are_listed_with_the_command_for_each` both leases belong to `w`, and in `test_holding_nothing_says_an_item_id_is_needed` no lease exists at all. So an implementation that ignores the agent id — e.g. agent `w` runs `ddflow heartbeat` while holding nothing, agent `x` holds T1, and it answers "needs an item id … heartbeat T1" instead of "holds no lease" — passes all three assertions, because every test uses the single agent `w` and never creates a lease owned by anyone else. A test seeding/claiming T1 as agent `x`, then running `heartbeat` as agent `w`, is needed to make the "the caller holds" promise non-vacuous.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_heartbeat_item_hint.py:20-47 (all three tests)

chunk_findings.detail: The "held" predicate is `it.lease.holder == me or _in_leased_tree(repo, it.lease.worktree, here)`, so any lease whose tree the caller merely stands in is selected as if the caller held it, and the refusal text hard-asserts the opposite ("{me} holds {len(held)} items"). Concrete input: agent `other` holds a lease on item `build` in tree `T`, agent `me` holds nothing and runs `ddflow heartbeat` (or `ddflow heartbeat ""`, which is exactly the shape of the original bug report) from `T`. `_the_held_item` computes `held == ["build"]`, `len(held) == 1`, and returns `("build", None)`, so the no-id branch proceeds to renew a lease the caller does not hold — silently extending `other`'s lease (defeating `services.leasebreak`'s idle/yield detection and keeping waiters blocked) instead of returning the promised `"heartbeat needs an item id ..., and me holds no lease"`. chunk_findings.detail:
The fallback that runs when the caller holds nothing by `holder == me` has no holder filter at all:

```python
held = sorted(i for i, ls in leased if ls.holder == me)
if not held:
    held = sorted(i for i, ls in leased if _in_leased_tree(repo, ls.worktree, here))
```

By construction, this branch can only ever fire on leases whose `holder` is *not* `me` (that is the only reason the branch exists), yet the value it produces is then treated as "what the caller holds": it is either returned as `item` (so heartbeat renews a lease the caller does not hold) or, when several match, rendered as ``f"{me} holds {len(held)} items -- `ddflow heartbeat {i}`..."``. Concretely: two agents share a repo root; agent A holds leases on `p` and `q` whose `worktree` is that root; agent B, holding nothing, runs `ddflow heartbeat` from the same directory. `held` for B is empty, the fallback collects `p` and `q`, and B is told "B holds 2 items -- `ddflow heartbeat p`, `ddflow heartbeat q`" — a statement that is false, and either the suggested commands fail (if the renewal path checks the holder) or B silently renews A's leases and prints "renewed p" (if it does not). Either way the message this change is meant to make accurate ("name the missing item id and list the items the caller holds") names items the caller does not hold, and the single-match case heartbeats an item that belongs to another agent; a lease's tree is not a sufficient proxy for ownership unless every lease in a shared worktree is deliberately co-owned, which the module docstring ("renews the lease for the holder") does not support.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new branch keys only off `o["item"] == item` and never compares `o["holder"]` with the claiming identity (`log.agent_id`). The added comment asserts "another agent holds it", but nothing in the code establishes that. The exact input from the folded-in report — a wait entry `{"item": "T1", "holder": "u5pin"}` recorded while `u5pin` is the agent running the command — now renders

    Recorded: T1 is waiting for its lease held by u5pin.

which is still a self-wait: T1 is waiting on the lease T1 already holds, and the holder named is the claimer itself. The requirement was "either report 'already leased to you' or name the real holder"; the code satisfies neither for the same-agent case (the holder it names is not a real external holder, and it never emits "already leased to you"). Because `WG.register` persists this text/entry, every later reader sees a nonsensical self-dependency and cannot tell whether `u5pin` is the claimer or a third party. chunk_findings.detail: The rewritten message calls the takeover command an inspection: "Inspect it with `ddflow recover --item {item_id}`; to take it over, run `ddflow recover --item {item_id}; ...`". `recover --item` is not read-only — it is the state-changing step that must be run before the `--force` claim can succeed (the same message repeats it as the takeover step). A user who runs it believing it is an inspection has already mutated the lease/worktree. The one-liner is also joined with `;` rather than `&&`, so when `recover` fails (e.g. the crashed agent's worktree no longer exists), the shell still proceeds to `ddflow claim {item_id} --force`, forcing a takeover whose prerequisite recovery just failed — the opposite of the "exact next command" promise this change is supposed to deliver.

chunk_findings.detail: The change's headline behaviour is untested: the intent says that when the EXPIRED lease belongs to the *same* agent identity, `claim` must renew it without `--force` (that is the three-command annoyance the task was filed for). The only expiry test in this file claims as agent "b" against agent "a"'s lease, i.e. the other-agent branch. Input that shows the gap: `DDFLOW_LEASE_TTL_S=1 claim T1 --no-worktree agent=a`, sleep past the TTL, then `claim T1 --no-worktree agent=a` — nothing here asserts exit code 0 on the renewal or the absence of the `ddflow recover --item T1; ddflow claim T1 --force` text, so a regression that keeps emitting the refusal/force sequence for the same identity (exactly the reported defect) passes this suite.

chunk_findings.detail: The folded DX-self-wait-wording item asks for either "already leased to you" or naming the real holder, and the reported wait record ("T1 is waiting for T1") comes from an item queued behind *itself*, i.e. the same agent re-claiming an item it already holds. This test only ever runs agent "b" against agent "a"'s lease and asserts the holder-naming sentence "waiting for its lease held by a"; the same-agent input (`claim T1 --no-worktree agent=a` while a holds/held the lease) is never issued, so the "already leased to you"/self-wait branch is unverified and the wording that produced the bug report can regress unnoticed.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new branch keys only off `o["item"] == item` and never compares `o["holder"]` with the claiming identity (`log.agent_id`). The added comment asserts "another agent holds it", but nothing in the code establishes that. The exact input from the folded-in report — a wait entry `{"item": "T1", "holder": "u5pin"}` recorded while `u5pin` is the agent running the command — now renders

    Recorded: T1 is waiting for its lease held by u5pin.

which is still a self-wait: T1 is waiting on the lease T1 already holds, and the holder named is the claimer itself. The requirement was "either report 'already leased to you' or name the real holder"; the code satisfies neither for the same-agent case (the holder it names is not a real external holder, and it never emits "already leased to you"). Because `WG.register` persists this text/entry, every later reader sees a nonsensical self-dependency and cannot tell whether `u5pin` is the claimer or a third party. The fix rewrites the symptom instead of distinguishing the two cases the note called out.
